title: Big and small black holes seem to follow the same rule for blasting jets
summary:
Black holes come in very different sizes. Some weigh about 10 times as much as the Sun, while others weigh millions of times more. Now astronomers say both kinds seem to follow the same rule when they shoot powerful jets of material into space.

The study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy. It was led by Dr. Adelle Goodwin of Curtin University's International Centre of Radio Astronomy Research in Australia, with Dr. Andrew Mummery of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.

The scientists studied rare events called tidal disruption events, when a supermassive black hole pulls a star apart. Sometimes the black hole sends out a jet right away. Other times it stays quiet for months or even years before a jet suddenly appears.

"We were looking at these events and asking why the timing was so different," Goodwin said.

Using telescopes in Australia, the United States, India, South Africa and space, the team found an answer. The delayed jets appeared when the black hole's feeding rate dropped to a certain critical point. Scientists already knew that same point mattered for much smaller black holes.

The key idea came to the two researchers during a conversation in Madrid while they were attending a science conference.

Not everything near a black hole falls inside. Some material is launched back into space. "You can think of it as a black hole burp," Goodwin said, "except these burps can blast material across enormous distances and influence the galaxies around them."

The researchers say the rule could help astronomers predict when these outbursts will happen. It also supports the long-held idea that black holes of every size follow the same basic laws of physics.
why_it_matters: If black holes of every size follow the same physics, scientists can use small, fast-changing ones to understand giant ones that shape whole galaxies.

keywords.explanation: Black holes are places in space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.
Supermassive describes the largest black holes, which can weigh millions of times more than the Sun.
Tidal disruption events happen when a black hole's gravity stretches and pulls apart a star that gets too close.
A critical point is a special level at which something important starts to change.
Outbursts are sudden, powerful releases of energy or material.
Astronomers are scientists who study stars, planets and other objects in space.

background_read: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape once it crosses the edge.
Small black holes can form when huge stars collapse, while supermassive black holes sit at the centers of most large galaxies.
As gas or pieces of a star swirl toward a black hole, some material can be thrown back out in fast, narrow streams called jets.
Astronomers use telescopes that detect radio waves and other kinds of light to spot these jets, because the black hole itself cannot be seen.
